person: Denise Holloway is a 55-year-old school office secretary who also handles her widowed mother's Social Security, Medicare and retirement paperwork. Her own household has a health FSA and a dependent care FSA through the school district. Her 9-year-old grandson Eli lives with her, and she claims him as a dependent. The plan year ended 30 June and the run-out is still open. She keeps receipts, EOBs and plan letters in the same kitchen drawer as her mother's mail, and she is afraid of missing a deadline or being asked to repay money. She is careful, tired and wary of any screen that asks for numbers she does not understand.
stated_up_front: I got a letter from the FSA saying one of my card charges needs paperwork and there's some deadline, and I think there's money I can still claim. Can you look through my things and tell me what I have to do and by when? Please don't use any of my mother's information, this is just mine.

facts.about: Her health FSA plan year and run-out
facts.truth: The plan year ended 30 June 2026. She believes the letter said claims are open through the end of October, but she is not sure of the exact day.
Her dentist's EOB shows she owes $148.00 on a crown done 12 March 2026. The insurer paid the rest.
Her EOB shows she owes $60.00 for a shoulder physical therapy visit on 21 April 2026.
Walgreens receipts show an allergy medicine for $18.49 on 3 May 2026 and first aid supplies for $12.30 on 17 May 2026. She bought both without a prescription and paid with her own debit card.
Eli's summer day camp was $320.00 in June 2026. After-school care at his school was $240.00 for April and May. Invoices came by email.
A $71.25 FSA card charge at a vision and ear clinic on 9 June 2026 is flagged as needing paperwork. The letter says to answer by 28 October.

facts.about: Things she paid for that she thinks might not count
facts.truth: A teeth whitening kit for $39 and a $34 monthly gym membership, both on her credit union statement. Also her $55 monthly multivitamins and her own Medicare supplement premium for her mother, which she does not think belong to her.
Her 17-year-old granddaughter Marisol sometimes babysits Eli and was paid $90 in cash. A visit for her 14-year-old nephew was also in the pile.
An orthodontic visit for Eli of $85 was paid with the FSA card in February, so it is already covered and should not be claimed again.
None of it belongs in this chore. Denise does not want her mother's Social Security number or bank details typed anywhere.

unknowns: The exact last day the plan accepts claims and whether the 28 October swipe date is a hard cutoff
Whether a visit in January before her coverage began, or a dental visit in July, can be claimed
Why whitening, vitamins and the gym are not eligible, and what happens if she claims one by mistake
Whether the EOB alone is enough to answer the pending card charge, or whether the plan also needs something from the clinic
